strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: spatial reasoning from ordinary monocular video without requiring depth-sensor input or an explicitly precomputed 3D map.

VLM-3R is technically plausible and clearly motivated. It combines frozen CUT3R geometry and camera tokens with appearance tokens through cross-attention, allowing reconstruction priors to be incorporated into a 7B video-language model.

The targeted instruction corpus is substantial (207,779 QA pairs), and the proposed VSTemporalI-Bench adds 138,610 QA pairs covering camera displacement/direction and camera-object or object-object relations.

The reported results are strong: VLM-3R obtains 60.9 average on VSI-Bench versus 40.9 for the strongest listed open-source baseline, and 58.8 on VSTemporalI-Bench versus 44.0 for the strongest listed open-source baseline.

A same-backbone, same-training-data comparison is included: VLM-3R scores 60.90 versus 57.74 for fine-tuned LLaVA-NeXT-Video, supporting a useful—though much smaller than the headline comparison—benefit from the proposed spatial fusion.
The supplementary material provides useful architectural dimensions, optimization settings, hardware requirements, task distributions, and descriptions of the automated QA-generation pipeline.
weaknesses: The central model-effectiveness claim is substantially confounded by targeted supervision. The large headline gains compare VLM-3R, trained on more than 200K task-specific spatial examples, against mostly untuned general-purpose models. Under the controlled fine-tuned comparison, the architecture contributes only 3.16 average points, and no variance or significance analysis is reported.

The manuscript does not establish scene-level and source-level separation between training and evaluation. Both the instruction data and VSTemporalI-Bench are generated from ScanNet, ScanNet++, and ARKitScenes, but the split procedure and scene identities are unspecified. Since questions are automatically generated from common templates, possible scene or template leakage is a material concern. The relationship between these training sources and VSI-Bench evaluation scenes is likewise not documented.

VSTemporalI-Bench supports a narrower claim than its name and discussion suggest. All environments are static, three of five tasks are single-frame spatial queries, and the two temporal tasks concern only camera displacement or direction. Thus it does not evaluate independently moving objects, interaction dynamics, event evolution, or general spatiotemporal reasoning.

Evaluation on the authors' benchmark is not controlled fairly: VLM-3R is fine-tuned on its 132,568-example training split, whereas the listed proprietary and open-source baselines appear to be evaluated without equivalent benchmark-specific tuning. There is no data-only fine-tuned baseline or component ablation reported on VSTemporalI-Bench.

The benchmark construction has unresolved validity issues. Camera 'distance traveled' is defined using Euclidean endpoint displacement, which differs from traveled path length for curved trajectories. The paper also provides no manual audit, annotation-agreement study, noise estimate, template-bias analysis, or cross-dataset generalization test for the automatically generated questions.

The ablations only weakly isolate the proposed components: removing geometry changes the average from 60.90 to 59.46 and removing camera tokens to 59.09, while some individual tasks improve after removal. There is no reconstruction-feature alternative, explicit point-map baseline, token/fusion design comparison, or run-to-run uncertainty.

Absolute metric inference from monocular RGB is intrinsically ambiguous and may depend heavily on learned dataset priors. Because training and testing draw from the same indoor dataset families and no held-out-domain evaluation is given, the evidence does not justify broad claims of reliable or scalable metric spatial understanding.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the supplied hyperparameters: the manuscript omits exact scene splits, most QA templates and thresholds, frame-sampling policy, evaluation prompts and decoding settings, the exact CUT3R checkpoint, LoRA target modules, random seeds, and a precise definition of the stated 'exact (or possible fuzzy)' answer matching.

The novelty is moderate rather than decisive: the core architecture is a straightforward reuse of frozen pretrained reconstruction tokens followed by cross-attention into an existing video LMM, and the claimed 'first' positioning is insufficiently differentiated from closely related reconstructive and position-aware 3D/video LMMs such as ROSS3D and Video-3D LLM.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: metric spatial reasoning directly from monocular video, without requiring depth sensors or a precomputed map at inference time.
The proposed combination of frozen CUT3R geometry/camera tokens with appearance tokens through cross-attention is technically plausible and integrates naturally with an existing video-language model.

The automated data pipeline is potentially useful: it produces 207,779 spatial-training QA pairs and a 138,610-pair benchmark spanning camera motion, camera-object distance, and viewpoint-relative object relations.

The reported results are substantial: VLM-3R reaches 60.9 average on VSI-Bench versus 40.9 for the strongest listed open-source pretrained baseline, and 58.8 on the new benchmark versus 44.0 for the strongest listed open-source baseline.

A same-data fine-tuned baseline provides some evidence beyond comparison with off-the-shelf models: VLM-3R improves over fine-tuned LLaVA-NeXT-Video from 57.74 to 60.90 on VSI-Bench. Component ablations and several training hyperparameters are also reported.
The authors explicitly acknowledge that the new benchmark contains only static scenes and that monocular reconstruction may be insufficiently precise for fine-grained object-size estimation.
weaknesses: The main empirical evidence has an unresolved leakage risk. Training QA, VSTI QA, and benchmark evaluations draw from ScanNet, ScanNet++, and ARKitScenes, but the paper never states that scenes, videos, or physical environments are disjoint across training and test sets. For automatically templated questions, a QA-level rather than scene-level split could permit near-duplicate frames, objects, and trajectories across splits. The reported split tables give only question counts, so the large gains cannot be confidently interpreted as generalization.

The VSTI comparison is not controlled for training exposure. VLM-3R is explicitly fine-tuned on the benchmark training set, whereas the listed proprietary and open-source baselines appear to be evaluated off the shelf. No baseline is fine-tuned on the same VSTI data, and no architecture ablation is reported on VSTI. Consequently, the benchmark's headline improvement does not isolate the proposed spatial tokens from task-specific supervision.

The VSI-Bench headline comparison similarly conflates architecture and data: most baselines are pretrained models, while VLM-3R receives 207K task-aligned examples. The controlled comparison against a fine-tuned LLaVA baseline shows a much smaller 3.16-point average gain, and the individual camera- and geometry-token ablations improve the average by only 1.81 and 1.44 points, respectively. No repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance analysis establish that these smaller architectural gains are robust.

The benchmark overstates temporal understanding. Three of its five tasks are labeled frame-level, all environments are static, and the two sequence tasks concern only camera displacement and coarse translation direction. It therefore does not support broad claims about understanding dynamic 3D environments, evolving object states, or general spatial-temporal reasoning.

Benchmark validity is insufficiently studied. There is no human validation of automatically generated annotations or templates, analysis of ambiguous visibility and occlusion cases, template-bias baseline, answer-only baseline, cross-dataset generalization, or deduplication analysis. Large numbers of QA pairs generated from relatively few scenes do not by themselves demonstrate diversity or difficulty.

The novelty is moderate: the principal modeling contribution is a one-layer cross-attention fusion of latent features from an existing reconstruction model and an existing video LMM. Calling the system 'end-to-end' is also potentially misleading because both visual and CUT3R encoders are frozen, and the approach still depends on a substantial pretrained reconstruction subsystem.

The evidence for practical scalability is incomplete. Training uses 16 H200 GPUs, yet the paper provides no parameter count for added modules, inference latency, memory use, throughput, or comparison with explicit-reconstruction pipelines. Thus, claims of better scalability and suitability for time-sensitive applications are unsupported.

Reproducibility has material gaps: the displayed project URL is blank; code and data availability are unspecified; scene-level split identities, frame-sampling procedure, relation thresholds, QA filtering, fuzzy-match rules, prompts, decoding settings, and complete baseline protocols are missing. The base-model naming is also inconsistent between the main text and appendix.

The ablation interpretation is occasionally stronger than the evidence. Removing geometry tokens changes absolute-distance performance only from 49.38 to 49.27 and actually improves relative direction from 80.52 to 81.35, while removing camera tokens improves relative distance from 65.35 to 62.82 only negatively but has mixed effects elsewhere. The paper lacks qualitative failure analysis or reconstruction-quality correlations that would substantiate its causal explanations.

Presentation issues—including inconsistent names such as VSTI-Bench versus VSTemporalI-Bench, grammatical errors, and dense figures—are correctable and are not the basis of the recommendation. The determining weaknesses are the unverified data separation, uncontrolled comparisons, and limited validation of the new benchmark. These outweigh the otherwise promising direction and favor weak rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: spatial reasoning directly from monocular video without requiring depth sensors or precomputed 3D maps. Integrating frozen CUT3R geometry and camera tokens with appearance features is technically sensible and potentially useful for robotics and embodied vision.

The empirical results on VSI-Bench are strong and broad. VLM-3R reaches a 60.90 average versus 40.90 for the best listed open-source baseline, with especially large gains in absolute distance, room size, relative direction, and route planning.

The controlled VSI-Bench comparison against a task-fine-tuned LLaVA-NeXT-Video baseline is valuable: adding the proposed 3D tokens and fusion raises the average from 57.74 to 60.90. Removing camera or geometry tokens also lowers the average, supporting the contribution of the spatial pathway beyond instruction data alone.

The work contributes substantial data resources: 207,779 spatial instruction examples and a 138,610-example benchmark spanning camera displacement, movement direction, camera-object distance, and object-object relations. Dataset construction, task definitions, counts, architecture dimensions, training hardware, and major hyperparameters are documented in useful detail.
weaknesses: Material: The evaluation protocol for VSTemporalI-Bench is insufficiently controlled. VLM-3R is fine-tuned on the benchmark's 132,568-example training set, whereas the manuscript does not report similarly fine-tuning the comparison models. Consequently, Table 2 cannot cleanly attribute VLM-3R's large advantage to its architecture rather than task-specific supervision.

Material: The benchmark split is described only through QA counts. The paper does not state that train and test sets are separated by scene, source video, or physical environment, even though many templated questions can be generated from the same scene metadata. Without an explicit scene-disjoint protocol and duplicate analysis, leakage and memorization remain significant concerns.

The claimed temporal scope is somewhat overstated. All benchmark scenes are static, only two of five tasks aggregate information across frames, and camera displacement is defined as endpoint Euclidean displacement rather than traveled path length. The benchmark primarily tests camera-motion and viewpoint-conditioned geometry, not general temporal reasoning involving independently moving objects or changing scenes.

The architectural evidence is promising but limited. The full model improves the matched fine-tuned baseline by 3.16 average points, yet only one backbone, reconstruction encoder, and benchmark are used for the ablation; no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or computational-efficiency comparison is provided. Some ablations also improve individual tasks, indicating that the roles of camera and geometry tokens are not uniformly established.

Originality relative to closely related reconstructive and position-aware models is not fully clarified. The method largely combines a pretrained CUT3R encoder, a standard cross-attention fusion block, LoRA tuning, and automatically generated instruction data; the distinctions from ROSS3D, Video-3D LLM, and other reconstruction-aware approaches deserve a more precise technical comparison.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the useful training appendix: frame sampling, benchmark scene allocation, filtering thresholds, fuzzy-answer matching, and full QA template/generation details are not completely specified, and the manuscript provides no concrete code, model, or dataset release commitment. There are also minor presentation issues, including inconsistent benchmark naming and several grammatical or notation errors, but these are readily correctable and do not drive the rating.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: metric spatial and camera-motion reasoning directly from monocular video, without requiring depth maps or preconstructed 3D maps at inference. Integrating frozen CUT3R geometry/view tokens into a video VLM is technically plausible and practically useful.

The main VSI-Bench comparison is reasonably well controlled. VLM-3R reaches 60.9 average versus 57.7 for the same 7B video model fine-tuned on the authors' 200K QA set, suggesting that geometry-aware fusion contributes beyond instruction data alone. Improvements are especially large for relative direction (80.5 versus 68.9) and room size (67.1 versus 63.7).

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering VSI-Bench, ScanQA, SQA3D, OST-Bench, Video-MME, VQAv2, and OpenEQA. The ScanQA/SQA3D results are competitive with methods that consume explicit 2.5D/3D inputs, while OST-Bench and OpenEQA provide some evidence of transfer beyond the generated training tasks.

The component and encoder ablations are informative: removing spatial or view tokens reduces VSI-Bench performance, explicit-point fusion underperforms latent-token fusion, and CUT3R improves the overall score from 57.7 to 60.9 compared with the fine-tuned base. The supplementary material also reports useful architecture dimensions, optimization settings, compute, and dataset-generation details.
weaknesses: Material concern: the VSTI-Bench comparison is not sufficiently controlled. The benchmark contains a 132,568-example training split, but the manuscript never clearly states whether VLM-3R was trained on it, nor whether any baseline received the same supervision. Comparing a benchmark-trained model against apparently off-the-shelf baselines would not establish architectural superiority; the exact training mixture for every reported VLM-3R result must be explicit for Table 2 to be interpretable.

Material concern: VSTI-Bench is presented as a temporal-reasoning benchmark, yet three of its five tasks are single-frame geometric queries, all scenes are static, and the two sequence tasks reduce to net camera displacement and dominant translation direction computed from poses. Thus, it does not test object dynamics, state changes, interactions, or richer temporal causality, and claims about general spatiotemporal reasoning are broader than the demonstrated evidence.

Material concern: benchmark validity and independence are underdocumented. The paper reports QA-level train/test counts but not numbers of scenes, videos, frames, or questions per scene; it does not explicitly document scene-disjointness for each source dataset in the detailed split description. Many automatically generated questions from the same scene and metadata can be strongly correlated. The unspecified relational threshold, filtering rules, annotation-quality audit, and human-evaluation protocol further limit confidence in the benchmark and the reported 77.0 human score.

The architectural novelty is moderate. The method largely combines an existing video VLM, an existing pretrained CUT3R encoder, one cross-attention block, and LoRA instruction tuning. The controlled gain over the equally fine-tuned 2D baseline is 3.2 average points, while removing individual token types changes the reported average by only about 1.4–1.8 points. No repeated runs, confidence intervals, or statistical analysis are provided to establish the stability of these smaller differences.

The central metric-scale claim lacks direct diagnostic support. The paper does not evaluate CUT3R's camera-pose or metric-depth errors on the benchmark videos, analyze how reconstruction errors propagate to answers, or test robustness to new camera intrinsics, outdoor scenes, scale distributions, or dynamic content. Current evidence is largely confined to static indoor datasets that overlap in source families across training and evaluation.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful supplementary details: the manuscript does not provide a code/data availability statement, exact frame-sampling and frame-count policies, complete prompts and output-parsing rules, random seeds, baseline inference settings, fuzzy-matching specification, or all QA-generation thresholds. Training is also described as configured for five epochs but stopped after one without explaining the stopping criterion.

Several internal reporting errors weaken confidence but appear correctable: Table 6 reports 59.09 without view tokens while the text says 50.09; Table 7's caption claims improvement over the base model in every category although counting drops from 63.1 to 49.6 and Agent Information from 58.3 to 58.1; and the base checkpoint is inconsistently called LLaVA-NeXT-Video and LLaVA-Video-7B-Qwen2. These are presentation/reporting flaws rather than standalone rejection grounds, but they require resolution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: metric spatial and camera-motion reasoning from ordinary monocular video, without requiring depth or preconstructed maps at inference time. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/bd3ac8fcf91b41108780570b5b6b0c9e/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The combination of frozen CUT3R spatial/view tokens with visual-token cross-attention is technically plausible and comparatively simple to integrate into a video VLM.

The automated data pipeline is substantial: it produces 207,779 spatial QA pairs, 4,225 route-planning examples, and a 138,610-example benchmark with scene-disjoint splits claimed to follow the source datasets.

Evaluation covers several settings. Against the identically data-tuned LLaVA-NeXT-Video baseline on VSI-Bench, the full model improves average accuracy from 57.7 to 60.9; it is also competitive on ScanQA/SQA3D and improves OST-Bench overall performance over its reported base model.
weaknesses: The evidence does not cleanly establish the architectural contribution. The central VSI-Bench gain over the same-data fine-tuned baseline is only 3.16 points, while the ablations report only aggregate accuracy, no uncertainty or repeated runs, and no task-level results for the principal spatial/view-token removals. The much larger gains over untuned models conflate the architecture with more than 200K task-specific training examples.

The VSTI-Bench results are especially difficult to interpret. The manuscript provides a 132,568-example training split but does not clearly state whether VLM-3R was trained on it, how it enters the final training mixture, or whether competing models received comparable supervision. Consequently, the reported 58.8 versus 40.0 base-model result cannot be attributed confidently to the proposed view-token design.

The new benchmark only partially measures temporal reasoning: three of its five tasks are single-frame geometric queries, all scenes are static, and the two sequence tasks reduce mainly to camera translation derived from poses. There is no analysis of language/template shortcuts, repeated correlated questions, per-scene effective sample size, or performance stratified by source dataset.

Benchmark construction is under-specified for reproducibility and validity. Important details such as relational thresholds, candidate and distractor sampling, visibility filtering, ambiguous-instance handling, numeric tolerances, scene counts, and human-evaluation sample size/protocol are absent or incomplete. Merely stating that standard source splits are followed does not rule out correlated templates or other leakage mechanisms.

Several quantitative claims conflict with the tables. The text says removing view tokens yields 50.09, whereas Table 6 reports 59.09. The VSI discussion cites gains from 20.2 to 49.4 and 12.3 to 67.1 using entries from a different base model, rather than the matched fine-tuned baseline. The OST-Bench text claims improvement across all categories, although object counting falls from 63.1 to 49.6 and Agent Information falls from 58.3 to 58.1. These are material reliability problems, not merely stylistic issues.

The method is incrementally novel: it largely uses latent tokens from a frozen pretrained CUT3R reconstructor and a standard residual cross-attention/projector. The paper does not compare sufficiently against equally trained alternative geometry-token fusion methods or test whether predicted poses, spatial tokens, and metric scale each provide independent benefits on VSTI-Bench.

The claim of eliminating reconstruction at inference is overstated: CUT3R is itself a recurrent learned reconstruction model that estimates metric point maps and camera poses, even if those explicit outputs are not passed to the language model. Runtime, memory, latency, video length, and scaling behavior are not reported, leaving the practical advantage over explicit reconstruction pipelines unsupported.

Training and inference details are inadequate for reproduction: only LoRA rank/scale, one epoch, and H200 hardware are given. Learning rate, optimizer, batch size, GPU count, frame-sampling policy, sequence length, LoRA target modules, dataset mixing for the main checkpoints, and evaluation decoding are missing. General-purpose performance also declines without mixed-domain data, and the supplemental OpenEQA result is lower overall than the base model. Overall, the worthwhile problem, dataset effort, and positive results are outweighed by confounded evidence, benchmark-validity gaps, inconsistent reporting, and incomplete reproducibility.

strengths: The empirical results support a meaningful contribution. With the same 200K instruction-tuning examples, VLM-3R obtains 60.90 on VSI-Bench versus 57.74 for the fine-tuned LLaVA-NeXT-Video control; CUT3R also obtains 60.9 versus 58.1 with VGGT. These controls indicate that metric-scale geometry and the proposed fusion provide benefits beyond training data alone.

The evaluation is broad, covering VSI-Bench, VSTI-Bench, ScanQA, SQA3D, OST-Bench, Video-MME, VQAv2, and zero-shot OpenEQA. Competitive results on depth-oriented 3D QA and improvement over the base model on OST-Bench provide useful evidence of transfer beyond the authors' generated benchmark.

The resource contribution is substantial: 207,779 spatial training QA pairs, including 4,225 route-planning examples, and VSTI-Bench with 138,610 QA pairs. The latter highlights the difficulty of metric camera-motion reasoning for current models.

The architecture is technically sensible and useful: frozen CUT3R spatial and view tokens are fused with visual tokens through a lightweight cross-attention module, enabling monocular RGB-video inference without sensor depth or precomputed 3D maps.

The paper is generally clear and includes important implementation information, including the initialization checkpoint, tuned components, LoRA configuration, optimizer settings, hardware, training duration, and a data-mixing experiment that largely restores general video performance.
weaknesses: VSTI-Bench is narrower than the paper's temporal-intelligence framing suggests. Three of its five tasks are single-frame spatial questions, while the sequence-level tasks cover camera displacement and dominant direction in static indoor scenes. It therefore primarily measures egomotion-aware spatial reasoning, not general temporal understanding of dynamic scenes.

Benchmark validation is underdocumented. The manuscript reports no manual audit of automatically generated questions, annotation-error or ambiguity rates, or sufficient methodology for the human-performance estimates. Generation choices such as relation thresholds and frame/sequence sampling are also incomplete. This is a material limitation because the benchmark is a central contribution.

The architectural originality is moderate relative to recent geometry-augmented VLMs: the method combines an existing CUT3R encoder, conventional cross-attention, and instruction tuning. The distinctive aspects are the metric-scale and camera-view tokens and the associated resources rather than a fundamentally new learning formulation.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the supplied hyperparameters. Evaluation prompts and decoding, exact video-frame sampling, seeds or variance, inference cost, parameter counts, and a concrete code/data release are not provided. Training also requires 16 H200 GPUs, creating a substantial replication barrier.

There are reporting inconsistencies: Table 6 reports 59.09 without view tokens while the prose says 50.09; the base model is variously named LLaVA-Video-7B-Qwen2, LLaVA-NeXT-Video, and LLaVA-Video-7B; and the OST-Bench text claims improvement across all categories although Agent Information is 58.1 versus 58.3 for the listed base. These appear correctable but reduce confidence in the current manuscript.

The claim of avoiding runtime reconstruction needs qualification because inference still runs the large pretrained CUT3R reconstruction encoder, even if no explicit point cloud is materialized. Without latency and memory comparisons against explicit reconstruction or competing geometry-augmented VLMs, the claimed deployment advantage is not established.
